subtopic_detail: Two exacerbations in a year on dual bronchodilator therapy with blood eosinophils of 0.4
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a sixty six year old retired shearer with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has smoked forty pack years and stopped two years ago.

He has had two exacerbations in the past twelve months, each needing prednisolone and antibiotics, with one overnight hospital stay. He takes a combined long acting muscarinic antagonist and long acting beta agonist inhaler and you have watched him use it correctly today. He walks more slowly than people his age on the flat and stops after about two hundred metres. He has completed pulmonary rehabilitation and is up to date with influenza and pneumococcal vaccination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Barrel shaped chest with reduced expansion, quiet breath sounds with a prolonged expiratory phase, no wheeze at rest, no peripheral oedema, body mass index 23 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Post bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in one second 45 per cent predicted with a ratio of 0.58, blood eosinophils 0.4 x10^9/L (0.0-0.5), alpha one antitrypsin within normal limits, chest radiograph shows hyperinflation without focal change

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to his inhaled therapy?

options.text: Continue the current inhaler and add long term azithromycin three times weekly after checking the corrected QT interval and hearing
options.rationale: Macrolide prophylaxis is an option for continued exacerbations despite optimised inhaled therapy, particularly in former smokers, but it comes after triple therapy rather than before it. It also carries risks of hearing loss, arrhythmia and resistance. (Source: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines)
source_refs: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines

options.text: Change to a combined inhaled corticosteroid and long acting beta agonist inhaler, stopping the long acting muscarinic antagonist component he now takes
options.rationale: Withdrawing the muscarinic antagonist removes a bronchodilator with proven exacerbation reduction in this disease and would represent a step backwards. Escalation means adding the steroid, not exchanging one component for another. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory

options.text: Change to a single inhaler containing an inhaled corticosteroid with both a long acting muscarinic antagonist and a long acting beta agonist
options.rationale: Adding an inhaled corticosteroid to dual bronchodilator therapy reduces exacerbations in people with frequent exacerbations and a blood eosinophil count at this level, and a single device preserves adherence. The eosinophil count is the biomarker that identifies who benefits. (Source: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines)
source_refs: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines

options.text: Continue the current inhaler and add regular oral prednisolone at a low maintenance dose to reduce the frequency of further exacerbations
options.rationale: Maintenance oral corticosteroid causes osteoporosis, diabetes, myopathy and skin fragility without reducing exacerbation frequency, and it has no place in stable disease. Steroid exposure here belongs in the airway rather than the bloodstream. (Source: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines)
source_refs: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines

options.text: Continue the current inhaler and add regular oral theophylline with periodic measurement of the serum concentration to guide the dose
options.rationale: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic index, numerous interactions and modest benefit, so it sits well down the escalation sequence. It would be considered only after inhaled options have been optimised. (Source: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines)
source_refs: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines

explanation.summary: Australian management of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease follows the COPD-X framework, in which non pharmacological measures including smoking cessation, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination and a written action plan carry as much weight as inhaled therapy. Pharmacological escalation moves from a short acting reliever, to a single long acting bronchodilator, to dual long acting bronchodilators, with inhaled corticosteroid added for people who continue to exacerbate. The blood eosinophil count predicts who benefits from the inhaled corticosteroid, with little benefit below about zero point one five and progressively greater benefit above zero point three, so it is the biomarker used to make this decision. Inhaled corticosteroid in this disease raises the risk of pneumonia, which is why it is targeted rather than given to everyone. Before escalating, adherence, inhaler technique and the diagnosis itself are checked, and where exacerbations continue on triple therapy the options include long term macrolide therapy or referral for specialist assessment.
key_points: Escalate to triple therapy when exacerbations continue on dual bronchodilators.
Blood eosinophil count identifies those who benefit from an inhaled corticosteroid.
Inhaled corticosteroid in this disease increases pneumonia risk, so it is targeted.
Check adherence and inhaler technique before every escalation.
Maintenance oral corticosteroid has no role in stable disease.
explanation.pearls: A single combination device is preferred to two or three separate inhalers wherever possible, because each additional device roughly halves the chance of correct daily use, and mixed device types with different inspiratory flow requirements are a common hidden cause of apparent treatment failure.

sources.label: COPD-X Plan: Australian and New Zealand guidelines

subtopic_detail: Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder and weight loss in a seventy year old
stem:
You are the physician seeing a seventy year old woman referred by her general practitioner with three weeks of yellow eyes. She has no abdominal pain and no fever, but describes itching that keeps her awake, dark urine and pale stools.

She has lost 7 kg over two months without trying and her appetite has fallen. She drinks minimal alcohol, takes no regular medications and has had no previous abdominal surgery. Her abdominal ultrasound reports a dilated common bile duct and intrahepatic ducts with a distended gallbladder and no stones seen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Deeply jaundiced with scratch marks over the arms, smooth non tender palpable gallbladder below the right costal margin, liver edge not enlarged, no ascites, no palpable lymph nodes
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 210 micromol/L (less than 20), alkaline phosphatase 620 units per litre (30-110), gamma glutamyl transferase 480 units per litre (5-35), alanine aminotransferase 96 units per litre (5-35), international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.9-1.3), ultrasound shows dilated intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts with no stones

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Percutaneous liver biopsy to establish a tissue diagnosis, with staging imaging arranged once the histological result is available for review
options.rationale: Biopsying the liver in obstructive jaundice yields only the secondary changes of obstruction unless a metastasis is targeted, and a coagulopathy from prolonged cholestasis adds bleeding risk. Tissue, when needed, is best obtained by endoscopic ultrasound guided sampling after staging. (Source: GESA: Clinical guidance)
source_refs: GESA: Clinical guidance

options.text: Computed tomography of the abdomen using a pancreatic protocol with arterial and portal venous phases, before any attempt at biliary intervention
options.rationale: A dedicated multiphase study defines the mass, its relationship to the mesenteric vessels and the presence of metastases, and this staging determines whether the disease is resectable. Stenting first introduces duct wall inflammation and air that degrade the staging images. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Pancreatic cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Pancreatic cancer guidelines

options.text: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with brushings and placement of a biliary stent to relieve the obstruction and the associated itch
options.rationale: Drainage before staging compromises the imaging that determines operability and adds pancreatitis and cholangitis risk, and preoperative stenting is not routinely required when surgery can proceed promptly. It is appropriate for cholangitis or when surgery will be delayed. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Pancreatic cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Pancreatic cancer guidelines

options.text: Repeat abdominal ultrasound after an overnight fast with attention to the distal duct, to look for a stone that may have been missed on the first study
options.rationale: Ultrasound is poor at visualising the distal duct behind bowel gas and has already established that the obstruction is distal. Repeating it delays definitive imaging in a patient with weight loss and painless jaundice. (Source: GESA: Clinical guidance)
source_refs: GESA: Clinical guidance

options.text: Serum tumour marker measurement including carbohydrate antigen 19 point 9 and carcinoembryonic antigen, with imaging arranged according to those results
options.rationale: These markers rise with any biliary obstruction and lack the specificity to diagnose or exclude malignancy, so they cannot direct imaging. They are used for monitoring after a diagnosis has been established. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Pancreatic cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Pancreatic cancer guidelines

explanation.summary: Painless obstructive jaundice with weight loss in an older patient is pancreatic head or periampullary malignancy until proven otherwise, and the palpable distended gallbladder described by Courvoisier makes stone disease unlikely because a chronically inflamed stone bearing gallbladder is usually fibrotic and does not distend. The pattern of liver tests, with alkaline phosphatase and gamma glutamyl transferase raised out of proportion to the transaminases, confirms cholestasis. The correct next step is a multiphase pancreatic protocol computed tomography scan, which identifies the primary lesion, defines the relationship between tumour and the superior mesenteric and coeliac vessels, and detects metastatic disease, thereby determining resectability. Endoscopic drainage before staging degrades those images and is reserved for cholangitis, severe symptomatic itch or a planned delay before surgery such as neoadjuvant therapy. Tissue diagnosis is obtained by endoscopic ultrasound guided fine needle sampling when required, and all cases are discussed in a multidisciplinary meeting at a centre with hepatobiliary surgical expertise.
key_points: Painless jaundice with weight loss in an older adult suggests pancreatic or periampullary malignancy.
A palpable distended gallbladder argues against stone disease as the cause.
Multiphase pancreatic protocol computed tomography is the staging investigation of choice.
Biliary stenting before staging degrades imaging and is not routinely required before surgery.
Tumour markers cannot diagnose or exclude the condition and are used for monitoring.
explanation.pearls: Check the international normalised ratio and give vitamin K before any procedure in prolonged cholestasis, because absent bile salts prevent absorption of fat soluble vitamins and produce a coagulopathy that corrects within a day of parenteral vitamin K but causes serious bleeding if it is overlooked.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Pancreatic cancer guidelines

subtopic_detail: Eligibility for lung cancer screening in a current smoker with a thirty five pack year history
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a fifty eight year old woman for a routine review. She smokes fifteen cigarettes a day and has done so since she was seventeen, giving about thirty five pack years, and she has tried to quit twice.

She has no cough, no haemoptysis, no chest pain and no weight loss, and she is otherwise well with no significant medical history. Her sister was recently diagnosed with lung cancer and she has read that scans are now available to detect it early. She asks what she should do and whether a chest X ray would be enough.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation with no wheeze, no clubbing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, body mass index 26 kg/m2, no hoarseness
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, renal function and liver function within normal limits, spirometry shows a ratio of 0.74 with a forced expiratory volume in one second of 88 per cent predicted

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: She should have an annual chest radiograph instead, since it involves less radiation exposure and is more accessible in general practice than a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Chest radiography was tested in large randomised trials and did not reduce lung cancer mortality, because tumours are usually well advanced by the time they appear on a plain film. Lower radiation from a test that does not work is not an advantage. (Source: National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Program guidelines)
source_refs: National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Program guidelines

options.text: She is not eligible for screening because she has no respiratory symptoms, so she should be reviewed if cough, weight loss or haemoptysis develops
options.rationale: Screening by definition applies to asymptomatic people, and symptomatic patients require diagnostic investigation rather than screening. Waiting for symptoms defeats the purpose of early detection. (Source: National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Program guidelines)
source_refs: National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Program guidelines

options.text: She should be referred for sputum cytology and a serum tumour marker panel, with computed tomography arranged only if either of those results is abnormal
options.rationale: Sputum cytology and tumour markers have poor sensitivity for early disease and are not screening tests for this cancer. Using them as gatekeepers would miss most of the small peripheral lesions that screening is designed to find. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines

options.text: She should be referred directly to a respiratory physician for bronchoscopy given her family history, with imaging arranged by the specialist afterwards
options.rationale: Bronchoscopy is an invasive diagnostic procedure for a suspected central lesion, not a screening tool, and family history does not change the screening pathway for this cancer. Referral without imaging inverts the diagnostic sequence. (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines

options.text: She is eligible for low dose computed tomography through the national screening program, and you should also offer her structured smoking cessation support
options.rationale: The Australian program uses age, pack year history and current or recent smoking as its criteria, and she satisfies all three, with screening repeated at defined intervals while she remains eligible. Cessation support is offered alongside because it remains the single most effective risk reduction available to her. (Source: National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Program guidelines)
source_refs: National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Program guidelines

explanation.summary: Lung cancer causes more cancer deaths in Australia than any other malignancy, largely because most cases present at an advanced stage. Australia commenced a National Lung Cancer Screening Program in July 2025, offering biennial low dose computed tomography to asymptomatic people aged fifty to seventy without symptoms suggestive of lung cancer, who have a smoking history of at least thirty pack years and who currently smoke or have quit within the past ten years. The evidence comes from randomised trials showing a mortality reduction of around twenty per cent with low dose computed tomography, while chest radiography showed no benefit in equivalent trials. Results are reported using a structured nodule classification system that determines the interval to the next scan or referral for assessment, which limits investigation of the many benign nodules found. Screening is offered together with smoking cessation support, since cessation delivers a larger reduction in risk than screening does and the two are complementary rather than alternatives.
key_points: Eligibility rests on age, a smoking history of at least thirty pack years, and current or recent smoking.
Screening applies only to asymptomatic people, since symptoms require diagnostic workup.
Low dose computed tomography reduces mortality whereas chest radiography does not.
Structured nodule reporting determines the interval to the next scan or referral.
Cessation support is offered alongside screening and reduces risk more than screening alone.
explanation.pearls: Quitting is worth raising at every screening visit, because a screening participant who continues to smoke retains most of their excess risk, and the period around a scan is a recognised teachable moment when quit attempts are substantially more likely to succeed.

sources.label: National Lung Cancer Screening Program: Program guidelines
Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines
RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice

subtopic_detail: Postural dizziness and two falls in a frail older man taking eleven regular medicines
stem:
You are the physician seeing an eighty eight year old man in the outpatient clinic after two falls at home in the past month, both when getting up from a chair. He lives alone with support from his daughter and walks with a stick.

He takes perindopril, amlodipine, frusemide, metoprolol, doxazosin, mirtazapine, temazepam, oxybutynin, atorvastatin, aspirin and pantoprazole. His blood pressure was measured in a supine and standing position today. He has no chest pain, palpitations or blackouts, and his daughter says his memory is slightly worse over the past year. There is no history of Parkinson disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 58 beats per minute, blood pressure 148/70 mmHg lying and 106/58 mmHg after three minutes standing, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Frail with reduced muscle bulk, timed up and go test prolonged, no focal neurological deficit, no resting tremor or rigidity, cardiac examination normal with no murmur, lying and standing pressures as recorded
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 133 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate 42 mL/min/1.73m2, haemoglobin 118 g/L (130-175), electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the brain and carotid ultrasound to investigate the falls, and review his medicines once those results have been reviewed
options.rationale: Falls occurring on standing with a documented postural drop and a long list of culprit drugs do not require neurovascular imaging, and carotid disease does not cause falls of this pattern. Investigation of this kind delays the intervention that will actually help. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Falls prevention)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Falls prevention

options.text: Withdraw the medicines contributing to postural hypotension and falls in a staged plan, reviewing symptoms and blood pressure after each change
options.rationale: Several of his medicines act directly on the mechanisms that maintain standing blood pressure or impair balance and cognition, and staged withdrawal with review is the approach that identifies which changes help without destabilising him. Deprescribing has the strongest evidence of any intervention for drug related falls. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people)
source_refs: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people

options.text: Start fludrocortisone to support the standing blood pressure and continue his current regimen, reviewing him again in the clinic in six weeks
options.rationale: Adding a mineralocorticoid to counteract drugs that could simply be stopped compounds the polypharmacy and risks fluid overload, hypokalaemia and supine hypertension. Removing the cause precedes any pharmacological support. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people)
source_refs: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people

options.text: Prescribe graduated compression stockings and advise him to rise slowly from sitting, continuing all current medicines and reviewing in three months
options.rationale: Physical measures help at the margins but are poorly tolerated by frail older people and do not address a drop of this magnitude driven by five contributing drugs. Delaying review for three months leaves him at risk of a fracture in the interim. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Falls prevention)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Falls prevention

options.text: Refer him for consideration of a permanent pacemaker given the sinus bradycardia, with medication review deferred until after the cardiology assessment
options.rationale: The bradycardia is explained by a beta blocker in a man with no syncope and no conduction disease, so it is a medication effect rather than an indication for pacing. Referral would expose him to a procedure that treats an iatrogenic finding. (Source: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people)
source_refs: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people

explanation.summary: Falls in frail older people are multifactorial, and medication is the most readily modifiable contributor, with risk rising steeply as the number of regular medicines increases. This man is taking four antihypertensives including an alpha blocker and a diuretic, a sedating antidepressant, a benzodiazepine and an anticholinergic agent for bladder symptoms, and together these explain both the postural drop and the impaired recovery when he stands. Deprescribing proceeds in stages rather than all at once, prioritising the drugs with the clearest link to the presenting harm, with each change followed by review of symptoms, blood pressure and function, and with the patient and family involved in the decisions. Anticholinergic burden deserves particular attention because it contributes to cognitive impairment as well as falls, and the bladder anticholinergic here is a frequent culprit. Comprehensive assessment also covers vision, footwear, home hazards, vitamin D and strength and balance exercise, which has the best evidence of any non pharmacological falls intervention.
key_points: Medication review is the highest yield intervention for drug related falls.
Antihypertensives, alpha blockers, sedatives and anticholinergics are the usual contributors.
Withdraw in stages with review after each change rather than all at once.
Anticholinergic burden contributes to cognitive impairment as well as to falls.
Strength and balance exercise has the best evidence among non drug measures.
explanation.pearls: Measure the blood pressure after three minutes of standing rather than immediately, since the delayed drop is the one that causes falls on walking away from the chair, and an early reading taken at thirty seconds regularly misses it.

sources.label: NPS MedicineWise: Deprescribing in older people
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Falls prevention

subtopic_detail: Large primary spontaneous pneumothorax with minimal symptoms in a stable young man
stem:
You are the emergency physician seeing a twenty three year old university student with left sided chest discomfort that came on suddenly while he was sitting at his desk four hours ago. He is tall and slim, smokes occasionally and has never had this before.

He walked into the department unaided and is comfortable at rest, describing mild pleuritic discomfort and no breathlessness when sitting. He has no underlying lung disease, no recent trauma and no diving history. His chest radiograph shows a left pneumothorax with a rim of about 3 cm at the level of the hilum and no mediastinal shift. He lives ten minutes away with two housemates and has reliable transport.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Comfortable at rest and speaking in full sentences, reduced breath sounds at the left apex, trachea central, no surgical emphysema, no distended neck veins, chest wall not tender
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph shows a left sided pneumothorax with an interpleural rim of about 3 cm at the hilum, no mediastinal shift, no effusion, no underlying parenchymal abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer him for video assisted thoracoscopic surgery with pleurodesis during this admission to prevent recurrence, since the pneumothorax is large
options.rationale: Surgery is indicated for a persistent air leak, a second ipsilateral event, a first contralateral event or occupational reasons such as flying or diving, not for a first uncomplicated episode. Operating now would over treat a condition that often resolves without intervention. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance

options.text: Admit him for high flow oxygen by mask for twenty four hours with a repeat radiograph the next morning before deciding whether drainage is required
options.rationale: Supplemental oxygen modestly accelerates resorption and is used in admitted patients, but admitting a comfortable young man purely for oxygen is unnecessary when observation and outpatient review are safe. The admission adds cost without adding benefit. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance

options.text: Observe him for several hours and arrange outpatient review with a repeat radiograph, giving written advice about symptoms that require immediate return
options.rationale: Conservative management is supported for a stable patient with minimal symptoms regardless of the size of the pneumothorax, with a randomised trial showing non inferior lung reexpansion and fewer adverse events than intervention. Safe discharge depends on proximity, reliable transport and clear return advice. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance

options.text: Insert a large bore intercostal catheter connected to an underwater seal drain and admit him to the ward until the lung has fully reexpanded
options.rationale: A large bore tube causes more pain and more complications than smaller alternatives and is reserved for tension, haemopneumothorax or ventilated patients. Routine drainage of a stable primary pneumothorax has been superseded. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance

options.text: Perform needle aspiration in the department, and if the lung reexpands discharge him with follow up and advice about symptoms requiring return
options.rationale: Aspiration remains an accepted option and was the previous default for a large pneumothorax, but it offers no advantage over observation in a patient with minimal symptoms and introduces a procedural risk. It is chosen when symptoms warrant active intervention. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance

explanation.summary: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in people without known lung disease, characteristically tall slim young men, and smoking substantially raises the risk. Management has shifted over the past decade from size based algorithms toward a symptom based approach, after a randomised trial demonstrated that conservative management of moderate to large primary pneumothorax was non inferior to interventional management for lung reexpansion at eight weeks, with fewer adverse events and fewer days in hospital. A stable patient with minimal symptoms can therefore be observed and reviewed as an outpatient, provided they can return quickly and have been given clear advice about worsening breathlessness. Intervention, by aspiration or small bore catheter, is reserved for significant symptoms, physiological compromise, or secondary pneumothorax in a patient with underlying lung disease, in whom the threshold is much lower. Smoking cessation halves the recurrence risk, and patients are advised not to fly until resolution is confirmed and never to dive again unless definitive surgical management has been undertaken.
key_points: Management is guided by symptoms and stability rather than by radiographic size alone.
Conservative management is non inferior for a stable patient with minimal symptoms.
Intervention is reserved for significant symptoms, instability or secondary pneumothorax.
Surgery follows persistent air leak, recurrence or occupational indications.
Smoking cessation substantially reduces the recurrence risk.
explanation.pearls: Diving is contraindicated for life after a spontaneous pneumothorax unless definitive surgical pleurectomy has been performed and cleared by a diving medicine specialist, and flying is deferred until resolution is radiologically confirmed, usually about a week afterwards.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pneumothorax guidance

subtopic_detail: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia with a raised parathyroid hormone and preserved renal function
stem:
You are the physician seeing a fifty two year old primary school teacher referred with a high calcium level found when she was investigated for tiredness. She describes constipation, low mood and two episodes of loin pain over the past year, the second of which passed a stone she collected.

She takes no supplements, no thiazide diuretic and no lithium. Her mother had a parathyroid operation in her sixties. A bone density scan performed last month showed a T score of minus 2.1 at the distal third of the radius. She has had no fractures.

data_table.Examination: Well appearing with no palpable neck mass, no bony tenderness, no proximal weakness, abdomen soft with no renal angle tenderness, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.90 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), parathyroid hormone 11.8 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), phosphate 0.68 mmol/L (0.75-1.50), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 90 mL/min/1.73m2, twenty four hour urinary calcium raised, vitamin D 68 nmol/L (above 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Observe with annual calcium, renal function and bone density measurement, advising generous fluid intake and avoidance of calcium supplements
options.rationale: Surveillance is appropriate for asymptomatic disease that fails to meet operative criteria, and she meets them on two counts. Continuing to observe accepts further stones and bone loss that surgery would prevent. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Start an oral bisphosphonate to protect her skeleton and review the calcium in three months before deciding whether any further treatment is required
options.rationale: Bisphosphonates improve bone density in this condition but leave the hypercalcaemia and stone risk untreated, so they are an adjunct for patients who cannot have surgery. They do not address the underlying adenoma. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Check the urinary calcium to creatinine clearance ratio and reassure her if it is low, since this pattern suggests a benign familial condition needing no treatment
options.rationale: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is an important differential and the ratio is the right test for it, but her urinary calcium excretion is already known to be raised. Her stone disease also argues strongly against that diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Refer her for parathyroidectomy after localisation imaging, since she has symptomatic disease with a kidney stone and reduced bone density
options.rationale: A documented kidney stone is an operative criterion in its own right, and she also has symptoms attributable to the hypercalcaemia, so surgery offers cure where medical therapy does not. Localisation with ultrasound and sestamibi scanning guides a targeted operation rather than establishing the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Start cinacalcet to lower the calcium level and monitor her calcium and renal function every six months in the outpatient clinic thereafter
options.rationale: Cinacalcet lowers calcium but does not improve bone density or prevent stones, and it is reserved for people in whom surgery is contraindicated or has failed. Using it in an operable patient trades cure for indefinite medical therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

explanation.summary: Primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in the community and is usually detected incidentally on a biochemistry panel. The diagnosis rests on a raised or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone in the presence of hypercalcaemia, typically with a low phosphate and raised urinary calcium excretion, and the main differential is familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, which is distinguished by a low urinary calcium to creatinine clearance ratio and which needs no treatment. Parathyroidectomy is the only curative treatment and is indicated for symptomatic disease and for asymptomatic patients who meet criteria including age under fifty, a calcium above the upper reference limit by a defined margin, an estimated glomerular filtration rate below sixty, nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis, marked hypercalciuria, or osteoporosis or vertebral fracture. Localisation imaging with ultrasound and sestamibi scanning is performed to plan a targeted operation and never to make the diagnosis, since a negative scan does not exclude an adenoma. Medical options such as cinacalcet and bisphosphonates are reserved for people who are not surgical candidates.
key_points: Hypercalcaemia with a raised or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone establishes the diagnosis.
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is excluded by urinary calcium excretion.
Surgery is the only cure and is indicated by symptoms, stones, osteoporosis, renal impairment or young age.
Localisation imaging plans the operation and does not make the diagnosis.
Cinacalcet and bisphosphonates are for patients who cannot have surgery.
explanation.pearls: The distal third of the radius is the site to watch on bone densitometry in this condition, because parathyroid hormone preferentially resorbs cortical bone and the forearm can be osteoporotic while the spine, which is mostly trabecular, still reads as normal.
